title: Secure E-Commerce Transactions
subtitle: A Cryptographic Case Study (BCS703)
author: Group Case Study - Cryptography & Network Security

bullets.text: Card-not-present fraud is the dominant attack on e-commerce.
Card numbers, CVVs, and customer PII travel over public networks every second.
Attackers exploit weak TLS, stored-card theft, man-in-the-middle, replay and tampering.
PCI-DSS mandates end-to-end encryption and integrity controls for cardholder data.
A single compromised record can mean regulatory fines, chargebacks and brand damage.

slides.title: Why Cryptography Alone Is Not Enough

bullets.text: Confidentiality without integrity = attacker can flip encrypted bytes blindly.
Integrity without authenticity = any sender can claim to be a legitimate customer.
Symmetric crypto is fast but cannot safely exchange keys across the Internet.
Asymmetric crypto solves key exchange but is too slow for full payloads.
Solution: HYBRID encryption + signatures + hashing, layered for defence-in-depth.
Protect customer payment information and transaction details from cyberattacks during online shopping.
Specific sub-problems to solve:
P-1  Confidentiality of card number, CVV, and customer PII in transit.
P-2  Integrity - any byte flip in the transaction must be detected.
P-3  Authenticity - the receiver must know the message came from the claimed customer.
P-4  Non-repudiation - a customer cannot later deny having sent the transaction.
P-5  Replay protection via a unique transaction ID and timestamp per request.
O-1  Build a working prototype that processes an end-to-end secure transaction.
O-2  Use industry-grade primitives: AES-256, RSA-2048, RSA-PSS, SHA-256, HMAC-SHA256.
O-3  Demonstrate confidentiality, integrity, authenticity and non-repudiation.
O-4  Show failure modes: a tampered envelope is rejected; a wrong key cannot decrypt.
O-5  Produce a reproducible Python implementation that can be demoed live.
AES-256 in CBC mode with PKCS#7 padding - encrypts the full transaction payload.
Random 128-bit IV generated per transaction - semantic security.
RSA-2048 OAEP / SHA-256 - encrypts the AES session key for safe transport.
RSA-PSS / SHA-256 digital signature - customer signs the payload.
SHA-256 hash - tamper-evident record of the payload.
HMAC-SHA256 - fast payment-token integrity check at the gateway.
All primitives come from PyCryptodome (FIPS-aligned algorithms).
Two parties: CUSTOMER (browser / app) and PAYMENT GATEWAY (server).
Each party holds an RSA-2048 keypair generated locally at session start.
Public keys are exchanged in advance (in production: signed X.509 certificates).
Customer builds a JSON payload: items, amount, card, customer, timestamp, txn_id.
Payload is signed -> encrypted with AES-256 -> AES key wrapped with RSA -> sent.
Gateway unwraps key -> decrypts -> verifies HMAC -> verifies signature -> approves.

rows: Customer signs plaintext JSON with RSA-PSS
Customer encrypts JSON with random AES-256 key + IV
AES key is encrypted with gateway RSA-2048 public key
Ciphertext + IV + wrapped key + signature + HMAC -> envelope
Gateway unwraps AES key with its RSA-2048 private key
HMAC + RSA-PSS verified, then APPROVE or REJECT

bullets.text: Language: Python 3.11
Library: PyCryptodome (AES, RSA, PSS, SHA256, HMAC)
File: secure_ecommerce.py (single-file, runnable end-to-end demo)
Modules: build_transaction_payload, customer_sends_transaction, gateway_processes_envelope
Test scenarios: happy path, tampered ciphertext, wrong private key
Output: human-readable log + JSON envelope for inspection
h = SHA256.new(raw)
signature = pss.new(customer_priv).sign(h)
aes_key = get_random_bytes(32)   # AES-256
iv, ct = aes_encrypt(aes_key, raw)
wrapped = PKCS1_OAEP.new(gw_pub, hashAlgo=SHA256).encrypt(aes_key)
mac = hmac.new(aes_key, token_input, hashlib.sha256).digest()
aes_key = PKCS1_OAEP.new(gw_priv, hashAlgo=SHA256).decrypt(wrapped)
raw = aes_decrypt(aes_key, iv, ct)   # raises on bad padding
payload = json.loads(raw)
if not hmac.compare_digest(mac_recv, mac_calc): REJECT
pss.new(customer_pub).verify(SHA256.new(raw), signature)
return {auth_code, status: 'APPROVED', amount, txn_id}

bullets.text: Hybrid encryption gives speed (AES) AND safe key exchange (RSA) in one design.
Digital signature adds authenticity and non-repudiation - a layer encryption alone cannot provide.
CBC's error-propagation is a useful side-effect for tamper detection in this design.
A unique IV per transaction is critical - never reuse an IV under the same key.
In production, AEAD (AES-GCM) would replace AES-CBC + HMAC for a single primitive.
Real systems add TLS for transport, X.509 certs for identity, and 3-D-Secure for cardholder auth.
A complete secure e-commerce transaction prototype was implemented and verified.
All five security objectives (confidentiality, integrity, authenticity, non-repudiation, replay protection) were met.
The design correctly rejects tampered ciphertext, forged HMACs, forged signatures, and wrong keys.
Defence-in-depth (RSA + AES + HMAC + signature + hash) prevents single-point failures.
Future work: swap CBC for AES-GCM (AEAD), add TLS, integrate X.509 certificates and a real payment gateway API.
William Stallings, Cryptography and Network Security - Principles and Practice, 8th Edition, Pearson.
NIST FIPS 197 - Advanced Encryption Standard (AES).
NIST FIPS 180-4 - Secure Hash Standard (SHA-256).
NIST FIPS 186-4 - Digital Signature Standard (RSA-PSS).
RFC 8017 - PKCS #1: RSA Cryptography Specifications Version 2.2.
RFC 2104 - HMAC: Keyed-Hashing for Message Authentication.
PyCryptodome Documentation, https://pycryptodome.readthedocs.io.
PCI-DSS v4.0 - Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard.
Questions are welcome.
